Lux Meter

📐 AT the point you want to check
Hold the phone at eye height where you normally sit, work, or read. Keep the light sensor uncovered and point its side toward the light field you want to check (usually the screen/front side). If you choose the camera fallback, face the camera into the room rather than directly at a bulb.
A laptop may not expose a light sensor. Its camera can make a relative estimate, but a phone light sensor or real lux meter is preferable.

shells.initial:
Flicker Detector

📐 AT the source
Point the camera directly at the bulb / fixture from ~30–50 cm, so the source fills a noticeable chunk of the frame. Rolling-shutter bands are harder to see after light reflects off walls or skin.
⚠ A user-facing webcam under-reads flicker — modulation amplitude attenuates when bouncing off your face. Use a phone for a real read.

Rolling-shutter bands can reveal some modulated lights. No bands does not prove a light is flicker-free, and this camera cannot report a reliable flicker frequency.

shells.initial:
Sleep Darkness Meter

📐 FROM your sleeping position
Place the phone face-up on your pillow or bedside table at night, lens facing the ceiling. Check the light field at your sleeping position with the room set as you normally sleep (door, hallway light, alarm clock, and curtains included).
⚠ A monitor webcam in a different room can't measure your bedroom darkness. This one needs to be physically on the bed.

Set the room as you actually sleep. The camera check is qualitative; enter a meter reading below for lux.

shells.initial:
Color Temperature

📐 AT the source
Point the camera directly at the fixture or a white wall lit by it from ~30–50 cm. White paper or a grey card under the source also works.
⚠ A user-facing webcam can be skewed by skin, clothing, automatic white balance, and the display. Use a phone aimed at a neutral surface when possible.

Approximate warm/cool camera check. It cannot show spectral completeness, red/infrared content, or melanopic EDI.

shells.initial:
Window / Glass Transmission

📐 TWO-STEP — same direction both times
Step 1: hold the camera against the closed window (looking out at the sky / scene). Step 2: same direction, but with the window open or stepping outside, so only the glass changes between readings.
Webcam can't do this — it can't physically move outside.

⚠ Aim at the same patch of sky / light source for both readings. North-window through the glass vs. east-window without it measures scene difference, not glass transmission.

📐 TWO-STEP — same direction both times

📐 FROM your position, at eye height
Hold the phone at eye height, facing forward while you walk through each room. The pause-detection captures the lighting where you actually look — not the floor or ceiling.
Walking with a phone is the whole point — a fixed webcam misses the inter-room comparison this tool exists to provide.
